papers.title_in_file: Who can sample forever? Shot noise effects in quantum linear regression
papers.version_note: arXiv:2610.12015v1 [quant-ph] 8 Oct 2026; 15 pages of main text, 25 pages of Supplemental Material (S1 to S40 numbering, references included).
papers.what_it_is: A theory-and-simulation paper showing that finite-shot estimation makes non-variational quantum linear regression (quantum extreme learning machines, fidelity kernels) ill-conditioned, and deriving the bias, variance and target-noise terms of the prediction error as functions of shots per state, training-set size and test shots.

The 'quadratic' decrease is of the squared bias term.
existing.value: The authors report, for quantum extreme learning machines trained by the unregularized pseudoinverse with exact training targets, that finite sampling produces a systematic prediction error whose squared bias decreases as the inverse square of the shots per state N, while the fluctuations from the random training measurements decrease inversely with the total training budget N times ntr, so that at fixed N more training states leave a bias floor; they state this holds provided the leading coefficients are nonzero and the stated conditioning and growth assumptions hold, and their proof of the two-term law is in a joint limit where N and ntr both grow with ntr/log(2 + N) growing.

assertions.value: The authors define quantum linear regression as the non-variational setting in which a fixed quantum device generates features that a classically trained linear model combines, covering quantum fidelity kernels and quantum extreme learning machines, with the features estimated from a finite number of shots.
quotes: Quantum fidelity kernels and quantum extreme learning machines share the same basic architecture: a fixed quantum device generates features that are combined through a classically trained linear model.
We refer to this broad non-variational setting as quantum linear regression.

assertions.value: The authors identify two regimes: for N at least of order ntr the MSE is dominated by training fluctuations and scales as the inverse of N times ntr; for N below ntr it is dominated by a quantum-induced systematic bias scaling as the inverse square of N; beyond ntr of order N the MSE saturates at a floor set by the per-state measurement statistics.

assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's summary of its Theorem 8 and numerics; the regime boundaries are scalings, not exact thresholds.

assertions.value: The authors state that in classical linear regression with exactly known features the least-squares bias is exactly zero in the underparametrized regime when the design has full rank, whereas in the quantum setting, even in the analogue of that regime, the pseudoinverse estimator acquires a systematic bias at finite N because shot noise changes the rank of the design matrix.

assertions.value: The authors state that the finite-statistics bias is the quantum counterpart of the attenuation bias of errors-in-variables regression and that the noise term acts as an implicit Tikhonov regularizer, with two features specific to the quantum setting: the noise strength is set by the per-state measurement budget under the experimenter's control, and the noise also populates directions orthogonal to the span of the ideal features.

assertions.value: The authors state that the test variance is a noise floor at fixed test budget M that no amount of training data can remove, though it can be suppressed by increasing M, and that even the ideal readout has this residual test error; they interpret it as an additional irreducible noise source specific to the quantum setting.
